faq.q: What makes current flow through something?
faq.a: Current only flows when there is a voltage difference, a push, between two points and a path joining them. Being at a high voltage is harmless if everything you touch is at that same voltage.
asks: Why does electricity need a voltage difference?

faq.q: Why doesn't the electricity go through the bird?
faq.a: The wire is a far better conductor than the bird, and both feet are on the same wire at almost exactly the same voltage. With no push across its body, the current stays in the wire.

faq.q: When are power lines dangerous to birds?
faq.a: Large birds with wide wings can touch two wires at once, or a wire and an earthed pole. Then there is a big voltage across them and current flows. Power companies fit covers and spacers to protect them.
asks: Do birds ever get electrocuted on power lines?

faq.q: Could a person hang on a power line like a bird?
faq.a: Never try it. Touching anything earthed at the same time, like a ladder, a tree or the ground, completes the circuit, and high-voltage lines can even arc through the air to people nearby.
asks: Is it safe to touch a power line if I am not on the ground?

faq.q: How do line workers work on live wires?
faq.a: Some specialists are raised to the line's voltage while kept well away from anything earthed, so, like a bird, no current flows through them. It needs special suits, tools and training.
asks: How can people touch live power lines?

facts: Local overhead distribution lines in the UK commonly carry 11,000 volts.
Power companies fit insulating covers and wider spacing to protect large birds such as storks and eagles.
